mode: spec dry run: interview -> research -> spec, no Designer. The agent cannot ask the user, so it writes the interview questions it would ask with recommended defaults, assumes the defaults, and proceeds. Outputs: spec.md and checks/<variant>.json per variant.

evals.name: asphalt-chip-seal-shoulder
evals.prompt: I want a tileable Substance Designer material for a worn chip-sealed shoulder on a rural two-lane road, a few years after the chip seal went down: chips missing in places, some bleeding where cars drift onto it, gravel and dirt collecting at the outer edge. It's for a game environment. Can you work out what it should be physically and write the spec before we build anything?
evals.expected_output: A spec for a chip-seal shoulder with a physical scale, a layer model (chips in a binder membrane over the old surface and base), process cards whose removals reveal the layer beneath (binder, then old surface), traffic-driven flushing, edge-driven debris, sourced numbers, invariants with enforcement and numeric checks, and valid checks JSON.
expectations: States a physical tile size, 2048 px and the resulting mm/px, chosen so chips (a few mm) are at least 2-3 px wide or moved to a detail tile; every number that drives a target (chip size, embedment, albedo, depths) carries a source or an estimate tag

Layer model with depths: single-size chips in a binder membrane of stated thickness over an older surface; chip loss reveals black binder, and the older surface shows only where the binder has worn through (driven by depth or wear, not by an independent noise); never soil or base colour directly

Colour trend is physically right for chip seal: new chip seal shows the aggregate's colour (or is black if fog-sealed) and changes with age as binder shows or oxidises; it does not apply the dense-asphalt 'black when new, grey when old' curve unexamined

Each symptom has a stated mechanism that places it: flushing where traffic over-embeds chips (laid flat in the drift band), chip loss where chips are under-embedded or ploughed, edge debris by a stated transport process (runoff on the cross slope, ploughing, traffic); none is placed by uniform noise
Every wear process states which layer it acts on, whether it removes or adds material, and what it reveals beneath

Research cites at least two chip-seal-specific sources (e.g. a seal-coat handbook or chip-seal study), and the numbers that hard checks depend on are traced to a named source section or flagged as estimates
Invariants are stated with how the graph enforces them structurally and a numeric check for each
Tiling is a hard check with a target on every axis that should tile (a strip that repeats only along the road checks that axis)
A checks JSON file exists, parses, and every check uses a type and region that the validator accepts (no undefined regions, no empty-by-construction ring regions)

No hard check would fail a physically correct material (including the spec's own default), and every hard check measures the property in the rendered maps rather than the mask wiring: no deposit checked inside the mask it was multiplied by, no mask compared with a mask built from the same bands, no concentration whose driver is the deposit's own source mask
expectations_iteration_1: States a physical tile size, 2048 px and the resulting mm/px, and chooses it so the smallest key features (chips of a few mm) are at least 2-3 px wide or explicitly moved to a detail tile

Layer model: single-size chips partly embedded in a binder membrane over an older surface (or base); chip loss reveals the black binder membrane and then the older surface, never soil or base colour directly

Colour trend is physically right for chip seal: new chip seal shows the aggregate's colour (or is black if fog-sealed) and changes with age as binder shows or oxidises; it does not apply the dense-asphalt 'black when new, grey when old' curve unexamined
Bleeding/flushing is placed where tyres run (wheel tracks / the drift zone), and edge debris and dirt are placed by the edge, each driven by a stated physical driver rather than uniform noise
Every wear process states which layer it acts on, whether it removes or adds material, and what it reveals beneath
Numbers that drive targets (chip size, embedment, albedo, depths) carry sources or are marked as estimates
Research went beyond generic asphalt knowledge to chip-seal specifics, citing at least two chip-seal-specific sources (e.g. a seal-coat handbook or chip-seal study)
Invariants are stated with how the graph enforces them structurally and a numeric check for each
A checks JSON file exists, parses, and every check uses a type and region that the validator accepts (no undefined regions, no empty-by-construction ring regions)
No hard check would fail a physically correct material (e.g. no check that forbids dark sockets while requiring chip loss, no reversed coverage arguments)

evals.name: concrete-board-formed-wall
evals.prompt: Can you plan a weathered board-formed concrete retaining wall material for Substance Designer? Think a 1970s highway retaining wall: board grain still printed in the concrete, white efflorescence coming out of the lift lines and tie holes, some rust staining, decades of weather. Tileable, for a game. I want the physics worked out and a spec before building.
evals.expected_output: A spec for a board-formed retaining wall with layout fixed by the formwork (boards, form seams, tie holes, lift joints), a layer model (paste skin, mortar, coarse aggregate, rebar at cover), efflorescence and rust as deposits sourced at defects and running downward, sourced numbers, invariants with checks, and valid checks JSON.
expectations: States a physical tile size, 2048 px and mm/px, with whole layout repeats (board widths, tie spacing or lift height) or a stated way to avoid a lattice; every number that drives a target carries a source or an estimate tag, and concrete albedo is not taken uncritically as a single solar value

Board marks, form seams, tie holes and lift joints are fixed by the formwork and invariant under weathering, and per-board tone comes from the form and persists through decades of weathering (it is not only a removable surface skin)

Layer model for a formed face: paste skin over a mortar-rich zone over coarse aggregate, with reinforcement only at cover depth; weathering reveals sand then aggregate in the same wall, never a different material

Efflorescence is a deposit with a water source (lift lines, cracks, tie holes, joints) and rust originates at steel, both running downward; gravity is tested directly in the rendered maps (deposit below vs above its source), not by containment in the mask the deposit was multiplied by
Every wear process states which layer it acts on, whether it removes or adds material, and what it reveals beneath

Research cites at least two sources on formwork, tie holes, efflorescence or formed-surface finishes, and the numbers that hard checks depend on are traced to a named source section or flagged as estimates
Invariants are stated with how the graph enforces them structurally and a numeric check for each
Tiling is a hard check, and no singular feature (a crack, a seep, a stain) repeats at the tile size more densely than its real spacing allows
A checks JSON file exists, parses, and every check uses a type and region that the validator accepts (no undefined regions, no empty-by-construction ring regions)

No hard check would fail a physically correct material (including the spec's own default), and every hard check measures the property in the rendered maps rather than the mask wiring: no deposit checked inside the mask it was multiplied by, no mask compared with a mask built from the same bands, no concentration whose driver is the deposit's own source mask
expectations_iteration_1: States a physical tile size, 2048 px and mm/px, and the tile holds whole layout repeats (board widths, tie spacing or lift height) or explains how it avoids a visible lattice
Board marks, form seams, tie holes and lift joints are fixed by the layout (formwork) and are invariant under weathering; weathering never moves or widens them

Layer model for a formed face: paste skin over a mortar-rich zone over coarse aggregate, with reinforcement only at cover depth; weathering reveals sand then aggregate in the same wall, never a different material
Efflorescence is a deposit with a water source (lift lines, cracks, tie holes, joints) and it runs downward under gravity; rust stains originate at steel (ties or rebar) and run downward
Every wear process states which layer it acts on, whether it removes or adds material, and what it reveals beneath
Numbers that drive targets (tie spacing, board widths, cover, albedo, depths) carry sources or are marked as estimates; concrete albedo is not taken uncritically as a single solar value
Research went beyond generic concrete knowledge to board-formed or formed-wall specifics, citing at least two sources on formwork, tie holes, efflorescence or formed-surface finishes
Invariants are stated with how the graph enforces them structurally and a numeric check for each
A checks JSON file exists, parses, and every check uses a type and region that the validator accepts
No hard check would fail a physically correct material (e.g. no reversed coverage arguments, no deformation that breaks an envelope check)

evals.name: wood-cedar-deck-grey-and-oiled
evals.prompt: I'd like a weathered cedar decking material in Substance Designer: most boards have gone silver-grey, but a few have been re-oiled so there's a mix of grey and warm oiled boards. Screws, gaps between boards, a bit of checking. Tileable for a game. Please research it properly and write the spec first.
evals.expected_output: A spec for western redcedar decking with a layout (board widths, gaps, joist lines, fastener rows), a per-board finish state, a weathered layer model (grey skin over brown photodegraded wood over fresh wood), oil as a penetrating finish, sourced numbers, invariants with checks, and valid checks JSON.
expectations: States a physical tile size, 2048 px and mm/px, with whole layout repeats (board width plus gap across, joist spacing along); every number that drives a target carries a source or an estimate tag; tiling is a hard check
The grey vs oiled state is a per-board property from the layout (board ID / a maintenance mask), and a hard check reads the rendered colour per board against that state, not only the exported mask
Weathered layer model: a grey leached surface over brown/photodegraded wood over fresh wood; erosion and wear reveal the same board's deeper wood, never the gap

Oil is a penetrating finish that darkens and warms the wood and slows greying, not a raised film with a step at worn edges; the direction that physics fixes (oiled more saturated than grey) is a hard check, with the magnitudes soft

Western redcedar specifics are right: fresh cedar is warm reddish-brown and darker or more saturated than the grey surface, so no check assumes fresh/damaged wood is lighter than grey; grey and oiled colour targets cite measured values or are tagged as estimates
Fasteners sit in straight rows on joist lines (two per board per joist or the stated hidden-fastener alternative); checks run along the grain and stay inside one board
Research cites at least two sources on western redcedar weathering or deck oils/finishes, and the numbers that hard checks depend on are traced to a named source section or flagged as estimates
Invariants are stated with how the graph enforces them structurally and a numeric check for each
A checks JSON file exists, parses, and every check uses a type and region that the validator accepts (no undefined regions, no empty-by-construction ring regions)

No hard check would fail a physically correct material (including the spec's own default), and every hard check measures the property in the rendered maps rather than the mask wiring: no deposit checked inside the mask it was multiplied by, no mask compared with a mask built from the same bands, no concentration whose driver is the deposit's own source mask
expectations_iteration_1: States a physical tile size, 2048 px and mm/px, and the tile holds whole layout repeats (board width plus gap across, joist spacing along)
The grey vs oiled state is a per-board property from the layout (board ID / a maintenance mask), not a noise or blotch
Weathered layer model: a grey leached surface over brown/photodegraded wood over fresh wood; erosion and wear reveal the same board's deeper wood, never the gap

notes: Iteration 2 expectations (revised 2026-10-03 after the iteration-1 review). Expectations that passed for both conditions in iteration 1 were merged or made harder; three now test the iteration-1 skill fixes directly (tiling as a hard check, hard checks that read rendered maps, certain colour order). Iteration-1 expectations are kept in each eval's 'expectations_iteration_1'. With one run per condition, a single expectation flip is noise; read pass counts with that in mind.
